The experiments in the [report](../rapport/index.html#experiences) run on an ordinary CPU. The [thesis plan](../these/index.html#plan-experimental) calls for more: campaigns of tens to hundreds of 3D simulations, GPU training runs, and a record of every result. This page describes the ready-to-use infrastructure of the repository: the Python package `milady` and the `infra/` folder. You rent a machine, run `git clone`, and a single command installs everything.

::: note
[What has been tested]{.tag}
The whole pipeline has run end to end on a machine **without a GPU** (laptop, full Docker stack, Slurm templates executed with a simulated scheduler): the suite of 68 automated tests passes (66 passed and 1 skipped when measured with PostgreSQL and MinIO; the anchor test, added since then, also passes). What could **not** be run: a GPU card, a real Slurm cluster, Apptainer, and a VM rented from a provider. The [last section](#tests) details what has been verified and what remains to be verified on site.
:::

## Getting started {#demarrer}

Three targets share the same code, pinned dependencies, and the same data format; the VM and the cluster also use the same software image.

| Target | What for | Main command |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Cloud VM with GPU**, rented by the hour | 3D campaigns and training, without a computing center | `sudo infra/deploy/bootstrap_vm.sh` |
| **B. Slurm cluster** (Jean Zay, regional HPC center) | large campaigns, multi-node training | `python -m milady.sweep … --scheduler slurm` |
| **C. Laptop**, no GPU | development, tests, small grids | `make setup && make smoke` |

**On a cloud VM.** Create an Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 VM, preferably with the provider's "GPU" image (NVIDIA driver preinstalled), a 100 to 200 GB disk, and a firewall that opens only SSH. Then:

```bash
ssh ubuntu@VM_IP_ADDRESS
git clone https://github.com/knoel99/milady-2027.git && cd milady-2027
sudo infra/deploy/bootstrap_vm.sh
```

The script, which can safely be rerun, installs Docker and, if a GPU is present, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit; it generates random passwords in a `.env` file that is never committed; it builds the image (`milady:gpu`, CUDA 12.6, or `milady:cpu`); it starts the PostgreSQL database, the MinIO object storage, and the MLflow server; finally, it runs an end-to-end test (tiny 3D simulation, file, catalog, one training iteration, evaluation). Measured duration without a GPU, with Docker already installed: 3 minutes, including the image build. You can also pass the file `infra/deploy/cloud-init.yaml` when creating the VM, without logging into it, or deploy from your laptop with `infra/deploy/deploy_remote.sh ubuntu@IP`.

Then, from the VM:

```bash
make sweep CONFIG=infra/configs/palier2_abc3d.yaml      # simulation campaign
make train CONFIG=infra/configs/train_fm3d.yaml         # training (all GPUs, torchrun)
make eval  CONFIG=infra/configs/train_fm3d.yaml         # evaluation, results to the catalog
```

The web interfaces (MLflow, MinIO console, JupyterLab) listen only on the VM: you reach them through an SSH tunnel, `ssh -N -L 5000:localhost:5000 -L 9001:localhost:9001 -L 8888:localhost:8888 ubuntu@IP`.

**On a Slurm cluster.** The GPU image is converted into an Apptainer image (`make image-gpu && make sif`), then copied to the cluster. Each simulation of a campaign is one element of a job array (one GPU each); training launches one `torchrun` per node. The compute nodes of Jean Zay have no Internet access: the catalog is then an SQLite file on `$WORK`; the simulations are subsequently registered in the central database from their MFF files (`python -m milady.catalog ingest`), under the same identifiers. The models, evaluations, and jobs of the SQLite catalog are not transferred by this command. The guide [`README-slurm.md`](https://github.com/knoel99/milady-2027/blob/main/infra/slurm/README-slurm.md) gives the options specific to Jean Zay, checked against the IDRIS documentation.

**On a laptop.** `make setup` creates a virtual environment with pinned versions (68 s measured), and `make smoke RUN=local` runs the same end-to-end test with an SQLite catalog and local files (4 s).

## The processing pipeline {#chaine}

A campaign described in a YAML file becomes simulations, then files, then a dataset, models, and evaluations. Each step writes its record to the catalog under a unique identifier (UUID); the simulations, their files, and the models also carry the code commit (with a `-dirty` suffix if the working tree had been modified).

![**Figure 1 — A campaign's pipeline and its three targets.** **a**, A YAML campaign (here `palier2_tg3d`: 4 × 3 $(Re, Pm)$ points, $64^3$ grid) goes through seven modules; every stage writes its record to the catalog, fields and checkpoints go to object storage, and a simulation carries the same UUID in its file and in the catalog, so the simulations part of the catalog can be rebuilt from the files (`ingest`). The split of stage 5 follows `train_fm3d.yaml` (validation $Re = 100$, $Pm = 1$; test $Re = 50$, $Pm = 2$); the spectrum of stage 7 is illustrative. **b**, The same roles on three targets; on the cluster, whose nodes have no Internet access, files are copied to S3 storage and then ingested into PostgreSQL, while models and evaluations stay in the cluster's SQLite. Diagram drawn with the [schematic-figure](https://lgwrightlab.github.io/schematic-figure/) skill; sources in `figures/architecture/`.](../../figures/architecture/figure/out/architecture-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel diagram. At the top, seven numbered stages from left to right, each with a thumbnail and its module, linked by vertical lines to two horizontal bands: the catalog, where each stage writes a table, and the files, where fields.h5 and last.pt go. At the bottom, a table of three columns, laptop, cloud GPU VM and Slurm cluster, over four rows: execution, files, catalog, tracking; two dashed arrows go from the cluster to the VM."}

| Step | Module | What is produced | Where it is recorded |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Campaign | YAML file in `infra/configs/` | grid of physical parameters ($Re$, $Rm$, $Pm$…) | `campaign` table (YAML of the first launch; each launch keeps a frozen copy in `data/sweeps/`) |
| 2. Launch | `milady.sweep` | one task per grid point: locally, one process per simulation; with Docker, one container per simulation; on a cluster, a Slurm job array | `simulation` and `job` tables |
| 3. Simulation | `milady.sim` (3D MHD solver, PyTorch) | fields $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B})$ and diagnostics | MFF file; `diagnostic` table |
| 4. Storage | `milady.storage` | file `{campaign}/{uuid}/fields.h5`, never modified in normal use (`--force` rewrites it, and its SHA-256 checksum is then updated in the catalog), on S3, MinIO, or disk | `file` table (SHA-256 checksum, size) |
| 5. Dataset | `milady.train.data` (at the first training run, following `data.auto_dataset`; stored by `milady.catalog`) | selection of simulations and split into training, validation, and test sets | `dataset` and `dataset_member` tables |
| 6. Training | `milady.train.fm3d` | conditional flow matching on vector potentials; checkpoints | `model` table; MLflow (curves, hyperparameters) |
| 7. Evaluation | `milady.eval` | statistical and physical metrics of the generated fields | `evaluation` table; `v_eval_summary` view |

Since the simulation carries the same UUID in the file and in the catalog, the simulation part of the catalog (simulations, files, diagnostics) can be rebuilt or merged from the files alone (parameters, code, commit, file, diagnostics; the campaign name is given with `--campaign`, and the compute time, resources, and campaign YAML are not restored); datasets, models, and evaluations, by contrast, exist only in the catalog. This is what makes it possible to work on a cluster without network access.

## The data format {#format}

Each simulation produces a file in the **MFF** format (*MilaDy Field Format*): an HDF5 file that follows exactly the convention of [The Well](https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/data_format/) (Ohana et al., NeurIPS 2024), the reference collection of physics simulations for machine learning, and adds metadata prefixed with `milady_`.

```
fields.h5
├── attributes: dataset_name, grid_type, n_spatial_dims, n_trajectories, simulation_parameters…
│               milady_uuid, milady_code, milady_git_commit, milady_parameters (JSON)…
├── dimensions/          time, x, y, z
├── boundary_conditions/ periodic conditions along each axis
├── scalars/             physical parameters (Re, Rm, Pm…)
├── t0_fields/           scalar fields
├── t1_fields/           u, B: (trajectories, time, x, y, z, components)
├── milady_diagnostics/  energies, dissipations, helicities, growth rates, max |∇·u|, max |∇·B|
└── milady_spectral/     Fourier coefficients of the fields (periodic domains, optional)
```

Following The Well makes the data readable by the reference loaders and models of the community: we checked, by replaying the HDF5 accesses of the `WellDataset` loader (the_well 1.2.0) without running the package itself, that a 3D MFF file is read back identically. The `milady_*` attributes are invisible to a The Well reader and are validated by a JSON schema. A **Zarr** variant, with the same hierarchy, makes it possible to read a chunk of a file on S3 without downloading it. An extension is planned for the outputs of SFEMaNS (azimuthal Fourier modes on a meridional finite-element mesh), without destructive interpolation. The validation function detects corrupted files: the 18 corruptions tested (types, shapes, non-finite values, identifiers…) are all flagged, a NaN in the middle of a trajectory only by the full check (`validate --full`). Full specification: [`specs/format-donnees.md`](https://github.com/knoel99/milady-2027/blob/main/specs/format-donnees.md). Figure 2, in the [section on the solver](#solveur), links each part of the file to its column in the catalog.

## The results catalog {#catalogue}

The results of a thesis are relational: campaign, simulations, files, datasets, models, evaluations. They are stored in a **PostgreSQL** database (locally or on the VM), or in an **SQLite** file with the same schema on a laptop or on a cluster without network access.

| Table | Contents |
|---|---|
| `campaign` | name, description, full YAML configuration |
| `simulation` | physical parameters (indexed JSON), status, machine, GPUs and cores, duration, code commit |
| `file` | URI, SHA-256 checksum, size, number of snapshots |
| `diagnostic` | time series of the physical diagnostics |
| `dataset`, `dataset_member` | versioned datasets and their split |
| `model` | hyperparameters, dataset, MLflow run, checkpoint, commit |
| `evaluation` | metric, value, parameters, seed, number of samples |
| `job` | scheduler identifier (Slurm, Docker), status, logs |

The catalog is queried in SQL or from the command line. For example, the compute hours per campaign (GPU hours only if each simulation had its own GPU, as in a Slurm array; on a VM, `make sweep` runs up to `resources.max_parallel` simulations at once on the same GPU):

```sql
SELECT c.name, round(CAST(sum(s.wall_time_s * CASE WHEN s.n_gpus > 1 THEN s.n_gpus ELSE 1 END) / 3600.0 AS NUMERIC), 1) AS heures_gpu
FROM simulation s JOIN campaign c ON c.id = s.campaign_id
WHERE s.status = 'done' GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY heures_gpu DESC;
```

and, from the command line, `python -m milady.catalog sims --campaign palier2_abc3d --param Rm__gt=8` lists the simulations of a campaign above a threshold. The heavy files live in object storage with an S3 API: MinIO on the VM, or a provider's bucket so that they survive the deletion of the VM. Training runs are tracked by **MLflow**, self-hosted, and linked to the catalog through the run identifier.

## The solver, the campaigns, and training {#solveur}

**Solver.** `milady.sim.mhd3d` solves periodic 3D incompressible MHD with a pseudo-spectral method in PyTorch, on CPU or GPU: fourth-order Runge–Kutta with an integrating factor, dealiasing with the 2/3 rule, Leray projection of $\mathbf{u}$ and of $\mathbf{B}$, so that both divergences remain at machine precision. It has two modes: dynamic (coupled Navier–Stokes and induction equations, ABC, Taylor–Green, or random forcing) and kinematic (imposed flow, as in experiment [E3](../rapport/index.html#e3)). Several trajectories advance together on the same GPU. The energy balance $\mathrm{d}(E_u + E_B)/\mathrm{d}t = \text{injection} - \nu\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle - \eta\langle|\mathbf{j}|^2\rangle$ is checked by the tests. On the development CPU, one step takes 0.08 s at $64^3$ in dynamic mode (2 threads); no GPU timing is given, for lack of a GPU, and the command `python -m milady.sim.mhd3d bench --device cuda` measures it on site.

![**Figure 2 — The solver and what a simulation writes.** **a**, One step of `milady.sim.mhd3d`: curls taken in Fourier space, products $\mathbf{u}\times\boldsymbol{\omega} + \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}$ in physical space, back to Fourier space, 2/3 dealiasing, Leray projection of the momentum term, curl of the induction term; the Lawson RK4 integrates the diffusion exactly, with four right-hand-side evaluations per step. The mode planes show 11 points per direction (actual cutoff $|m| \le 21$ at $64^3$). **b**, One simulation of `palier2_tg3d` over time: diagnostics from $t = 0$, 40 snapshots over the kept window, checkpoints and resume after SIGTERM (example position). **c**, The MFF file follows The Well's convention (grey) and adds `milady_*` attributes and groups; the identifier, parameters, commit and diagnostics have their column in the catalog.](../../figures/solveur/figure/out/solveur-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Three panels. At the top, a loop between Fourier space, on the left, and physical space, on the right: spectral state, curls, inverse transform, products, forward transform, dealiasing, Leray projection and curl, then the Lawson RK4 that returns to the state. Bottom left, a timeline of simulated time from 0 to 140 with continuous diagnostics, 40 snapshots between 100 and 140, checkpoints and an interruption followed by a resume. Bottom right, the tree of an HDF5 file linked to three catalog tables."}

**Ready-made campaigns.** They prepare the tiers of the [thesis plan](../these/index.html#plan-experimental) at reduced scale: `palier1_mhd2d` reuses the E2 dataset ($32^2$, fixed $\nu$, 11 values of $\eta$), not yet the $128^2$ plan on an 8 × 8 $(\nu, \eta)$ grid; the 3D campaigns keep 20 to 40 snapshots per simulation, against about 5000 per point planned for tier 2.

| Campaign | Contents |
|---|---|
| `palier1_mhd2d` | forced 2D MHD from experiment E2: 11 values of $\eta$, 16 trajectories per value |
| `palier2_abc3d` | ABC kinematic dynamo at $64^3$: $Rm$ from 4 to 40 (37 simulations), magnetic eigenmodes |
| `palier2_tg3d` | Taylor–Green forced 3D MHD at $64^3$: $Re \in \{25, 50, 100, 200\}$ and $Pm \in \{0.5 ; 1 ; 2\}$ (12 simulations) |
| `train_fm3d` | flow matching of the Taylor–Green fields conditioned on $(Re, Pm)$, vector potentials truncated at $|\mathbf{m}| \le 8$, exact $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ symmetry |

**Training.** `milady.train.fm3d` carries over to 3D the choices validated by the experiments: vector potentials in the Coulomb gauge (zero divergence by construction, like variant V4 of E2), a velocity field equivariant under $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$ (variant C of E1), and optional fine-tuning with an unbiased estimate of the stationarity loss. Experiment E1 showed that this fine-tuning can diverge when started from a biased model: it is launched only from an already good model, with two safeguards added for this reason (disabled by default: they stay at 0 unless set), an anchor to the starting weights (`stationarity.anchor`) and a gradual ramp-up of the weight $\beta$ (`stationarity.beta_warmup`), and the spread of the balances must be monitored: the per-sample standard deviation of the balances is not yet computed automatically, because the evaluation records only the mean residuals. The same code runs on one GPU or on several nodes (DDP), resumes after an interruption from its last checkpoint `last.pt` when restarted under the same run name (`--run-name`, or `--resume <uri>`; automatically under Slurm only for a job requeued with the same ID), and logs to MLflow.

## Costs {#couts}

Prices change with the provider, the region, and the rental mode: the guide gives no prices, but a method.

$$
\text{cost} \approx \sum_{\text{tasks}} \text{duration (h)} \times \text{number of GPUs} \times \text{hourly price of the instance} \;+\; \text{storage} \;+\; \text{outbound data} .
$$

First measure a single representative simulation; its duration is recorded in the catalog and extrapolated to the whole campaign. As for memory, a state $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B})$ in single precision takes $6 \times N^3 \times 4$ bytes, i.e., about 0.4 GB at $256^3$; the peak memory measured on CPU is about 15 times this state at $128^3$ (717 MB), which comes to about 6 GB at $256^3$ and 48 GB at $512^3$: a 24 GB GPU is enough at $256^3$, and an 80 GB GPU is needed at $512^3$ (an estimate to be checked with `nvidia-smi`). Three rules reduce the bill: preemptible instances for the simulation arrays, which are independent and can be restarted; a VM deleted as soon as it is no longer in use, after a backup (`make backup`); and data in a bucket rather than on the VM's disk.

## What is tested, what remains to be verified {#tests}

| Verified on the development machine (no GPU) | Measured duration |
|---|---|
| laptop installation (`make setup`) and end-to-end test (`make smoke RUN=local`) | 68 s and 4 s |
| CPU Docker image built from scratch; PostgreSQL, MinIO, MLflow stack healthy | 2 min; 14 s |
| end-to-end test in the Docker stack: objects in MinIO, MLflow run completed, catalog populated | 10 s |
| installation by `bootstrap_vm.sh --cpu` (Docker already present) on a fresh copy of the repository, then a rerun | 3 min; 33 s |
| automated tests (`make test`), with PostgreSQL and MinIO | 66 passed, 1 skipped (before a 68th test was added, which also passes) |
| Slurm templates executed with a simulated scheduler, including stopping at the end of the time limit and resuming | a few seconds |
| MFF file read back by replaying the HDF5 accesses of The Well's loader; backup produced by `make backup` (`pg_dump` dumps and bucket mirror) | — |

Still to be verified on site, at the first rental: the full GPU image and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, the solver and training on CUDA (and on several GPUs), a real Slurm with Apptainer, the installation of Docker on a fresh Ubuntu, the providers' S3 buckets, and the campaigns at their real size. The [deployment guide](https://github.com/knoel99/milady-2027/blob/main/infra/README.md) (§ 11 and 12) gives the details.
